prompt:
A clean technical illustration (side elevation, no perspective) of a painted plywood classroom stacking set on a pale desk: a flat base with THREE upright pegs standing on it, marked A (left), B (middle) and C (right).

There are 5 rings of clearly different widths -- disk 1 (the narrowest) is red, disk 2 is yellow, disk 3 is green, disk 4 is blue, disk 5 is purple (the widest) -- and every ring has its own size number printed large on its face. The stacking rule is the usual one -- a disk rests either on the base or on a disk wider than itself, never on a narrower one.

The rings do NOT start in one tower. At the start they lie like this:
    - peg A holds, from the BOTTOM upward: disk 5, then disk 2, then disk 1
    - peg B holds, from the BOTTOM upward: disk 3
    - peg C holds, from the BOTTOM upward: disk 4

Someone now gathers all 5 rings onto peg C in the FEWEST possible moves -- the shortest way needs exactly 31 moves -- lifting one ring at a time, always the top ring of a peg, never putting a wider ring onto a narrower one. Every shortest solution stands in the SAME arrangement after move 17.

Show the board EXACTLY as it stands at that instant, immediately after move 17: not the starting layout, not the finished tower, not any other moment. Every ring must sit on the peg it really occupies then, in the correct order; a peg holding no ring must be drawn empty.

Keep the picture clean: no move list, no annotations, no captions. The only characters in the image are the letters on the base and the number printed on each ring.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show a painted classroom stacking set: a base with three upright pegs carrying round stacking disks of graduated widths? A realistic photo, an illustration, a schematic or a clean diagram ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image instead shows just a blank card or plain panel that prints an answer with none of that shown, or shows something unrelated. Answer yes or no only.

reference.q_notext: The peg letters on the base and the size number printed on each disk do not count. Apart from those, is there a separate line of text or numbers that lists moves or states where the disks sit? Answer yes or no.
